title: Episode 249: Sitting Bull: Tatanka Iyotake, the Sun Dance Vision, the Little Bighorn, and the Standing Rock
description:
The monumental life of Tatanka Iyotake—Sitting Bull: the supreme spiritual leader, war chief, and holy man of the Lakota Sioux nation. Refusing every treaty that ceded ancestral lands, Sitting Bull united the Lakota, Northern Cheyenne, and Arapaho in defense of the sacred Black Hills. In June 1876, following his prophetic Sun Dance vision of blue-coated soldiers falling like grasshoppers, Sitting Bull inspired the crushing defeat of General George Armstrong Custer's Seventh Cavalry at the Battle of the Little Bighorn. Enduring exile in Canada, forced reservation confinement, and world tours with Buffalo Bill Cody, Sitting Bull stood unbroken until his tragic martyrdom at Standing Rock in 1890. Discover the profound spiritual depth and tragic majesty of the greatest defender of the American Plains.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, our Top 50 Famous Non-President Americans series chronicles the supreme spiritual and political leader of the Lakota Sioux, whose courage, visions, and defiance echoed across the Great Plains and shook the American republic. Here is George with the life of Tatanka Iyotake: Sitting Bull.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE HOLY BOY ON THE GRAND RIVER: 1831
Born around 1831 along the wooded bottoms of the Grand River in what is today South Dakota, the boy who would shake the foundations of the United States was initially named Jumping Badger. Because of his deliberate, thoughtful demeanor and careful contemplation before taking action, his family nicknamed him 'Hunkesni'—meaning 'Slow'. Yet behind this quiet reserve lay a warrior of exceptional physical courage and deep spiritual reverence. At age fourteen, during a raid against the rival Crow nation, young Slow rode forward on his pony, struck an enemy warrior with his wooden coup stick, and took his first horse. His father, a respected Hunkpapa Lakota leader named Returns-Again, honored his son's bravery by giving him his own sacred ancestral name: Tatanka Iyotake—translated into English as 'Sitting Bull', signifying an unmovable buffalo bull planted solidly on his haunches, refusing to be moved by any threat. Sitting Bull excelled as a hunter, horseman, and protector of the elderly and orphans, earning entry into the elite Strong Heart and Silent Eaters warrior societies. From his earliest youth, Sitting Bull experienced vivid prophetic dreams and visions, spending days fasting on solitary buttes to commune with Wakan Tanka—the Great Sacred Mystery of the Lakota universe. From his earliest childhood, Jumping Badger was trained in the spiritual traditions of the Hunkpapa, learning from holy elders that a true leader must always be the first to sacrifice and the last to take food for himself.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE IRON HORSE AND THE BLACK HILLS: DEFYING THE TREATIES
By the 1860s, the flood of white gold prospectors, miners, and the iron locomotives of the Northern Pacific Railway were slicing through the heart of the northern Great Plains, driving away the massive buffalo herds upon which the nomadic Lakota way of life entirely depended. While other tribal leaders signed treaties accepting agency rations and confining their people to reservations, Sitting Bull adamantly refused every compromise. He declared that he had never touched the pen to surrender an acre of ancestral land, refusing to live on government hand-outs of spoiled beef and wormy flour. In 1868, the Treaty of Fort Laramie set aside the sacred Black Hills—Paha Sapa, the spiritual heart of the Lakota world—as an unceded, permanent Indian reservation forbidden to white settlement. But when Lieutenant Colonel George Armstrong Custer led a military expedition into the Black Hills in 1874 and discovered rich gold deposits, thousands of illegal prospectors flooded the sacred valleys. The United States government offered to purchase the Black Hills for six million dollars, but Sitting Bull famously retorted: 'One does not sell the earth upon which the people walk.' When the federal government issued an ultimatum ordering all non-reservation Lakota to report to agencies by January 1876 or be declared hostile enemies of the state, Sitting Bull ignored the demand, rallying thousands of free Lakota, Northern Cheyenne, and Arapaho families to his summer hunting encampment on the Rosebud River. Sitting Bull's refusal to sign the Fort Laramie treaties stemmed from an unshakeable moral conviction that the sacred earth, water, and buffalo belonged to future generations and could never be converted into commercial real estate.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE SUN DANCE VISION: SOLDIERS FALLING LIKE GRASSHOPPERS
In early June 1876, on the banks of Rosebud Creek in Montana, Sitting Bull conducted the sacred Sun Dance ceremony to seek divine guidance from Wakan Tanka for the coming war against the United States Army. For three days and nights without water or food, Sitting Bull danced around the sacred cottonwood pole, having one hundred pieces of flesh carved from his arms by his adoptive brother Jumping Bull as a holy sacrificial offering. Gazing directly into the blazing sun until he collapsed into an unconscious trance, Sitting Bull received a momentous prophetic vision: he saw a great swarm of blue-coated soldiers and horses falling upside down from the sky directly into the Lakota encampment, like dead grasshoppers dropping from the air. A powerful celestial voice spoke to him from the heavens: 'I give you these soldiers because they have no ears.' Sitting Bull awoke and delivered the holy prophecy to his people: a colossal military host of white soldiers was marching to destroy them, but the Great Spirit had already delivered them into the hands of the warriors. The vision electrified the encampment, inspiring the young war chiefs—including the legendary Oglala champion Crazy Horse—with absolute certainty of divine victory. The sacred Sun Dance on the Rosebud Creek was an act of supreme spiritual devotion, wherein Sitting Bull gave his own flesh and blood to petition Wakan Tanka for the survival and freedom of his people.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE BATTLE OF THE LITTLE BIGHORN: JUNE 25, 1876
In late June 1876, Sitting Bull's vast encampment moved west to the meandering banks of the Little Bighorn River—known to the Lakota as the Greasy Grass. It was the largest gathering of native people in the history of the Great Plains: over seven thousand Lakota, Cheyenne, and Arapaho men, women, and children occupying over one thousand tipis stretching for nearly three miles along the cottonwood groves. On the scorching midday of Sunday, June 25, Lieutenant Colonel George Armstrong Custer's Seventh Cavalry arrived at the ridge overlooking the valley. Recklessly dividing his six hundred troopers into three detachments without scouting the true size of the encampment, Major Marcus Reno attacked the southern end of the village, while Custer rode north along the ridges with two hundred and ten men to attack the center. Sitting Bull, now forty-five years old, remained in the village to direct the evacuation of women, children, and elders, while Crazy Horse, Gall, and two thousand screaming warriors counterattacked with devastating fury. Reno's men were routed into timber and besieged on a hilltop. Surrounding Custer's isolated battalion on the high dry ridges, the native warriors unleashed a storm of arrows and repeating rifle fire. In less than an hour of chaotic, swirling combat, Custer and every single one of his two hundred and ten men were annihilated, fulfilling Sitting Bull's Sun Dance vision to the exact letter. At the Little Bighorn, Sitting Bull's strategic calmness during the sudden cavalry assault allowed the war chiefs to coordinate their counterattack, turning what was intended as a massacre of native families into a historic triumph.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE BITTER FLIGHT TO CANADA: THE GRANDMOTHER'S LAND
The annihilation of Custer and the Seventh Cavalry stunned the American public, arriving just as the nation was celebrating its centennial of independence in Philadelphia. The federal government responded with overwhelming military vengeance: thousands of infantry and cavalry troops flooded the northern plains, confiscating native horses and systematically slaughtering the remaining buffalo herds to starve the free tribes into submission. Refusing to surrender his weapons or accept reservation life, Sitting Bull led two thousand starving Hunkpapa followers north across the international border into Saskatchewan, Canada, in May 1877—seeking sanctuary in the territory of Queen Victoria, known to the Lakota as 'the Grandmother'. Welcomed by Major James Morrow Walsh of the North-West Mounted Police, Sitting Bull established a peaceful encampment at Wood Mountain. For four years, the Canadian Mounted Police respected Sitting Bull's authority and dignity, but the tragedy of starvation proved inescapable: with buffalo herds exterminated across the border and Canadian rations non-existent, his people were reduced to eating their sled dogs, horses, and boiled moccasin leather. Deeply heartbroken by the cries of starving children, Sitting Bull returned south across the border in July 1881 and surrendered his rifle to Major David Brotherton at Fort Buford, declaring: 'Let it be recorded that I was the last man of my people to surrender my gun.' During the four harsh years of exile in Canada, Sitting Bull earned the deep respect of the North-West Mounted Police for his strict enforcement of peace, sharing what little food his camp possessed with starving refugees.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE WILD WEST SHOW AND THE GHOST DANCE: 1885 TO 1890
Following two years of military imprisonment at Fort Randall, Sitting Bull was transferred to the Standing Rock Agency in Dakota Territory. In 1885, he joined Buffalo Bill Cody's world-famous Wild West Show, touring eastern American cities and Canada. Audiences booed the famous chief as the murderer of Custer, but Sitting Bull maintained an aura of serene, regal majesty, earning fifty dollars a week and giving away almost all of his earnings to impoverished street urchins and beggars in New York and Chicago. Returning to Standing Rock, Sitting Bull watched in sorrow as the federal Dawes Act carved up reservation lands and disease ravaged his people. In 1890, a desperate religious movement swept across the plains: the Ghost Dance, preached by the Paiute prophet Wovoka, who promised that if the people danced in sacred circles, the buffalo would return, deceased ancestors would rise, and the white invaders would disappear. Indian Agent James McLaughlin at Standing Rock was terrified by the dance, viewing Sitting Bull as the dangerous ringleader of a new armed uprising, and resolved to arrest the holy man. When touring with Buffalo Bill Cody, Sitting Bull was greeted by cheering crowds in Montreal and Chicago, using his celebrity not for personal enrichment, but to remind the American public of the plight of his reservation people.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE TRAGIC MARTYRDOM AT STANDING ROCK: DECEMBER 15, 1890
At dawn on December 15, 1890, thirty-nine armed Indian Agency police officers surrounded Sitting Bull's wooden cabin on the frozen banks of the Grand River. Dragging the fifty-nine-year-old chief out into the freezing morning air in his nightclothes, the police attempted to force him onto a waiting horse. A crowd of enraged Lakota followers gathered outside, shouting at the police. A warrior named Catch-the-Bear pulled a rifle and shot Lieutenant Henry Bullhead in the side; as Bullhead fell, he fired a bullet into Sitting Bull's chest, while Sergeant Red Tomahawk shot the great chief in the back of the head. In the chaotic gunfight that erupted, Sitting Bull, his seventeen-year-old son Crow Foot, and six native police officers were killed in the snow. Fourteen days later, his terrified followers fled south, leading directly to the horrific Wounded Knee Massacre. Tatanka Iyotake died as he had lived: unbowed, unconquered, and fiercely protective of his people's freedom. Sitting Bull stands across world history as a titan of spiritual integrity: a leader who understood that a nation's soul is not measured by its wealth or armaments, but by its reverence for the earth and its unwavering courage to defend the sacred. Sitting Bull's martyrdom at Standing Rock was a tragic culmination of fear and misunderstanding, yet his sacred legacy as an unyielding defender of indigenous sovereignty and spiritual integrity remains immortal across the world.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories. Next week, our Top 50 Famous Non-President Americans series continues with Episode 252: Crazy Horse—Tasunke Witko, the Battle of the Rosebud, Custer's Last Stand, and the Unbroken Spirit. Until then, stay curious.
